--- title: "[Graph.set_node_attrs_ws()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Set attributes on all selected nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L13861-L13961){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.set_node_attrs_ws(**attributes) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Set attributes on selected nodes](/assets/graphs/set-node-attrs-ws.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Every node carries a value x in a badge (A 3, B 5, C 2, D 4, E 6, F 1). Nodes B, D, and F are selected in the accent color; after the call all three read 7, whatever they held before, while the other nodes keep their values." width="100%"} Writes one or more attributes onto every node in the current selection, modifying the graph in place. Each keyword argument names an attribute and gives the value that all selected nodes receive. Attributes not mentioned in the call are preserved, and existing attributes with the same name are overwritten. The selection itself is left unchanged, so further `_ws` methods can be chained. This is the "with selection" counterpart of `set_node_attrs()`, and it is handy for: - tagging nodes that match a condition (select first, then label them) - flagging the result of a traversal or neighborhood query - styling a subset of nodes (e.g., `color=`, `size=`) before plotting Every selected node gets the same value; to assign different values per node, use `set_node_attrs()` with a list or dict, or `mutate_node_attrs_ws()` to derive new values from existing ones. If no nodes are selected, the call does nothing (no error is raised). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [**attributes]{.doc-parameter-name} : Attribute name-value pairs to set on the selected nodes, e.g., `color="red", importance=0.9`. Each keyword becomes an attribute name and its value is stored as-is on every selected node. Because these are keyword arguments, names must be valid Python identifiers; use `set_node_attrs()` for names containing spaces or other characters. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Attributes are applied only to nodes currently in the selection. Here `A` and `B` are selected and receive `color` and `importance`, while `C` gets nothing: ::: {#7bfb83e9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes([("A", {"value": 10}), ("B", {"value": 20}), ("C", {"value": 30})]) ) id_a = graph.get_id_from_label("A") id_b = graph.get_id_from_label("B") ( graph .select_nodes_by_id([id_a, id_b]) .set_node_attrs_ws(color="red", importance=0.9) ) graph.get_node_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The original `value` attribute survives untouched on `A`, since this call never mentioned it: ::: {#7cc97fc2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node(id_a).attributes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'value': 10, 'color': 'red', 'importance': 0.9} ``` ::: ::: Combining this with `select_nodes()` makes it easy to select nodes matching a condition first, then tag only the matches (here, nodes with `value > 15`): ::: {#51e5fffd .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( graph .clear_selection() .select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes.get("value", 0) > 15) .set_node_attrs_ws(category="high") ) graph.get_node_attrs("category") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {2: 'high', 3: 'high'} ``` ::: :::
